summary:
## Key Concepts

- **Svelte vs Frameworks**: Svelte is a **compiler** that turns component files into optimized JavaScript at build time; React, Angular, and Vue ship framework/library code that runs in the browser alongside your app.

- **Bundle size & performance**: Svelte often produces the **smallest, highly optimized** bundles because no runtime framework code is shipped. React, Vue, and Angular can also be fast but typically produce larger bundles due to framework runtime.

- **Feature trade-offs**: Svelte and React focus on minimal core features (components, reactivity) and expect you to add HTTP, validation, routing, or state libraries as needed. **Angular** is the most complete, including router, HTTP client, validation, and enterprise-grade features. **Vue** sits between Angular and React with official router and state solutions (Vuex).

- **Developer ergonomics and runtime helpers**: React and Angular provide higher-level runtime helpers (e.g., Suspense, differential loading) that can automate tasks like loading states or browser-targeted bundles—capabilities Svelte’s compile-time model intentionally omits.

- **Community & maintenance**: React (Facebook) and Angular (Google) are corporate-backed and widely adopted; Vue is an established community project; Svelte is newer and primarily driven by its original author but growing quickly.

> [!TIP]
> Try Svelte for small projects or parts of a larger app when bundle size and straightforward syntax matter.

> [!NOTE]
> Learning Svelte improves general JavaScript and component-based thinking, but it may not be the best primary skill if your goal is job-market demand—React, Angular, and Vue remain more established.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Consider feature needs (routing, HTTP, validation), team familiarity, and long-term maintenance when choosing: Svelte for minimal, performant apps; Angular for full-featured enterprise apps; React/Vue for flexible ecosystems.
transcription:
## Svelte is a compiler, not a framework

Let's dive right in and let's have a look at it. So I want to compare Svelte to React, Angular, and Vue. Now the first important, very important distinction is that Svelte is actually a compiler, whereas the other free alternatives are frameworks or libraries. Now what does this difference mean? It means that with Svelte you also use a certain syntax to write your code. You also use a component-driven architecture. For example, you write markup, styles, and you write instructions in JavaScript. But then when you run your, when you build your app for production, you actually run the Svelte compiler automatically and that goes all over your code, all your code files, your entire project, and it creates a bundle JS file with a bunch of JavaScript instructions that will then execute in the DOM at runtime.

## What Svelte's compiled output means for bundle size and runtime

It does not add some extra code or extra package. It does not add any framework code which would execute at runtime. And that's different for React, Angular, or Vue. There, when you build your application, that code is also getting optimized and compiled during development to some extent, but then it works in conjunction with the library or framework package, React, Angular, or Vue. So you have to ship both your optimized application and the optimized framework code and that obviously means more code than just a bunch of instructions. And indeed, one of the advantages of Svelte is that it gives you a super small bundle. In this case, in this example, which you find in another video I created, it's only 4 kilobytes small. And if you would create a similar application with Vue, Angular, or React, you might still end up with small applications, but they would be bigger than that. So you have a very small code size which you get in the end. And that code is also highly optimized and very fast during production.

## Comparing performance and feature sets

So from these options, Svelte gives you the smallest and very fast bundles. Now React also gives you small and fast bundles. Angular also gives you medium-sized but also at runtime very fast bundles, fast code. And for Vue, we also have small and fast code. So it's not horrible for the other options, but they are certainly bigger than Svelte. So this is already all we have a clear winner, right? Well, that's not all. Actually, having a small bundle and having fast code of course matters, but it's not everything. In Svelte, you get a certain core set of features you can work with when you develop. You have a core syntax for outputting data, for reacting to events, and so on. But that's basically it. It's very similar in React. React is all about creating components and then rendering something to the screen and reacting to user input. For Angular and Vue, that would be different. There, for Angular for example you have a huge set of features. Angular includes its own HTTP client, validation, routing, all that stuff. Vue also has its own state management library Vuex and its own router though it does not include validation or its own HTTP client. So Angular is the completest solution, which is why it's extremely popular amongst enterprises. Vue is in between. React is very lightweight, focused on components and Svelte also is very lightweight, focused on components and on getting something onto the screen. If you need HTTP, you need to bring your own package or use the built-in fetch function. If you need validation, build it on your own or add some other JavaScript validation library. This is how it works. Also, Svelte doesn't give you any additional improvements. It gives you highly optimized code, but it does not give you extra features like React does, for example. There you have lots of additional improvements and more improvements to come over the year. Something like React Suspense and so on where React actively controls your code and how it runs and tries to optimize when the DOM is updated, might automatically display a loading spinner if you're waiting for some data. These are all some behind-the-scenes tasks where React helps you which Svelte doesn't give you. You also have additional or comparable improvements in Angular. Maybe not an automated loading spinner, but there you have features like differential loading, which means that Angular will give you a production-ready application which detects in which environment you're running, so in which browser, and depending on the browser the app is loaded into, it will load more or less code taking advantage of more or less modern JavaScript syntax. And Vue also has some additional improvements. For example, you can also create different bundles for different browsers. And therefore, these are all things which Svelte doesn't have. And that is what I meant. Small and fast bundles are nice, but of course, we also have to think about the ease of development with additional features. And also, if we're getting additional help for the application, which might actually improve the runtime experience for our users.

## Community, popularity, and maintainers

There is more than these points though. Let's have a look at popularity. Svelte is very popular, but also very new and small. If we have a look at the community, it's growing rapidly, especially over the last couple of months, and it's really gaining some traction, but of course, it's still small, especially compared to these alternatives. React is extremely popular and relatively mature. Of course, it's still highly actively developed. For example, React Hooks were just added a couple of months ago, but it's been there for a couple of years now. It's getting used by major big enterprises. It definitely is there to stay. It's the same for Angular. Angular also is extremely popular and also very mature. It's also getting used by a lot of enterprises and will not go anywhere. And Vue is also very popular, even more popular than Angular and React are, and it's not quite as mature but still relatively mature. It's maturing more and more and it's also getting used by more and more bigger companies. And compared to these alternatives, Svelte really is smaller, but I believe it's still worth a look. And I'll come back to this in a second. First of all, let's have a look at who's developing these solutions. And for Svelte, it's basically a one-man show. Rich Harris, employed at the New York Times, is developing it. It's open source, so you can contribute, but it's mostly him doing all the groundwork, the foundation work, and the development, especially in the past. For React it's obviously developed by Facebook, for Angular by Google and for Vue there is no big company developing it but it's actually an open-source team effort. Initially when it first came out it also was a one-man show by Evan You, but since then it matured and now it has a really big team splitting the work and working on Vue. So that has really developed into something bigger.

## When to learn and use Svelte

And now with that the obvious question is: should you learn it? And in my opinion Svelte is worth exploring or adding it to your next project. Svelte has a very intriguing syntax. It gives you very fast and small applications. It has some very interesting ideas which I haven't seen like this in the other frameworks and libraries. And even though it's small, it might definitely be worth a look. Now, to not give you any illusions, you'll probably not find a Svelte job posting. It's too small for that. But you might be able to use it in your next project. Suggest it to your decision makers in your company and maybe employ it in a smaller project, in a part of a project, or if you're working on your own alone. If you have a project you want to realize, well then you should definitely have a look at Svelte because it then really is a decent alternative to these other frameworks and libraries. Now, of course, if your primary goal is to get a job with what you learn here, then this Svelte knowledge might help you get a better understanding for JavaScript in general, and it also has similar concepts like React and Angular and Vue does. So it might still help you there. But of course, React, Angular, and Vue will be your better options, your better alternatives because these are all established, especially React and Angular, and Vue is also more and more establishing. So if that is the primary goal, jobs, well then take the other ones. If you want to explore something exciting new though, if you're working on your own, if you want to suggest it in your company, or if you simply want to broaden your horizon and get a better JavaScript developer, then Svelte definitely is worth a look, and I would strongly recommend learning it.
